{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"Choice screens are not market choice

A menu is not a market

A choice screen is supposed to give people control. It’s the screen that asks which browser, search engine, assistant, or application they want to use. The stated promise is simple: show the alternatives, let the user decide, and allow competition to work.

But who selected the alternatives? The answer is usually the company that controls the device, operating system, or distribution channel (the apps, services, or stores). That company decides which options appear, which disappear, and which are placed first (often before anyone reads the screen). The user receives a menu, but the gatekeeper has already drawn its borders.

This doesn’t make every choice screen useless. It does mean the screen itself cannot be treated as proof of a competitive market. A restaurant can offer ten dishes and still control the kitchen, the prices, and the ingredients. A device maker can offer several services while controlling the road by which each service reaches the buyer.

Defaults do the quiet work

The first option is rarely just the first option. It is the one that requires no additional search, no unfamiliar permission, and no interruption in the task that brought someone to the screen. Many people will keep it, not because they compared every alternative, but because changing it costs attention (a resource the interface is designed to conserve).

The effect is practical. A default can shape discovery, habit, data flows, and future switching. It can determine which account is created, which service receives information, and which application becomes familiar before a rival has a fair opportunity to be tried. The screen may say that the user is free to choose, while the surrounding system makes one choice feel like the natural continuation of the purchase.

A company may call this convenience. Convenience matters, and it’s not a trivial benefit. But convenience cannot be separated from control when the same company selects the options, writes the interface, and governs the path to installation (a browser, operating system, or app store). What looks like a neutral prompt may be a carefully positioned continuation of the company’s own design.

The menu can preserve the gatekeeper

Nominal choice is choice in name. It gives the buyer a visible alternative without necessarily changing the conditions under which alternatives compete. If every listed service depends on one operating system, one account, one payment channel, or one approval process, the central power remains in place (even when every option is technically available).

That power can persist after the moment of selection. The gatekeeper may still decide which services are interoperable, which updates are permitted, which defaults return after an upgrade, and which costs attach to leaving. A person can select a rival and still encounter a system built to make the rival peripheral.

What does that choice mean if the selected service cannot reach the same users, use the same device functions, or compete on the same terms? The question is not whether an alternative appears on the screen. The question is whether the alternative can operate without asking the gatekeeper for special treatment.

A legal disclaimer won’t solve that problem. A disclaimer can describe a menu; it cannot create an open market. Nor can a company claim that every option is equal when its own defaults determine what people see first, what they learn to use, and what they must overcome to leave (the button the interface presents as normal).

A remedy must change control

A meaningful remedy would change the structure behind the screen. It would require access on fair terms to the functions and distribution routes that make a service viable (a company’s preferred route). It would limit the ability to reset a chosen default, bury a rival, or make switching costly through design. It would also require clear disclosure of who selected the options and what the gatekeeper still controls.

That remedy should not force every person to make a complicated decision at every turn. We’re asking for a market in which a simple choice has consequences beyond the appearance of choice. We’re also asking lawmakers to measure competition by what firms can do after selection, not by how many names fit inside a prompt.

The governing principle is straightforward: a choice screen is meaningful only when the choices can compete. If the system still controls access, defaults, data, and switching, the menu is a smokescreen (not merely a menu). Lawmakers should not impose remedies that leave that structure untouched, and they should not mistake a visible list for public control (including the cost of switching). If you want that principle enforced, contact the lawmakers responsible for the rules and ask what power the screen leaves in the gatekeeper’s hands.","omitted":[{"habit":"opponents-allies-sources / o11; dimension: opponents-allies-sources","why":"The request supplies no verified opposing position, named ally, or source to attribute; adding one would require inventing material."}],"refused":""}

structured_output.draft:
Choice screens are not market choice

A menu is not a market

A choice screen is supposed to give people control. It’s the screen that asks which browser, search engine, assistant, or application they want to use. The stated promise is simple: show the alternatives, let the user decide, and allow competition to work.

But who selected the alternatives? The answer is usually the company that controls the device, operating system, or distribution channel (the apps, services, or stores). That company decides which options appear, which disappear, and which are placed first (often before anyone reads the screen). The user receives a menu, but the gatekeeper has already drawn its borders.

This doesn’t make every choice screen useless. It does mean the screen itself cannot be treated as proof of a competitive market. A restaurant can offer ten dishes and still control the kitchen, the prices, and the ingredients. A device maker can offer several services while controlling the road by which each service reaches the buyer.

Defaults do the quiet work

The first option is rarely just the first option. It is the one that requires no additional search, no unfamiliar permission, and no interruption in the task that brought someone to the screen. Many people will keep it, not because they compared every alternative, but because changing it costs attention (a resource the interface is designed to conserve).

The effect is practical. A default can shape discovery, habit, data flows, and future switching. It can determine which account is created, which service receives information, and which application becomes familiar before a rival has a fair opportunity to be tried. The screen may say that the user is free to choose, while the surrounding system makes one choice feel like the natural continuation of the purchase.

A company may call this convenience. Convenience matters, and it’s not a trivial benefit. But convenience cannot be separated from control when the same company selects the options, writes the interface, and governs the path to installation (a browser, operating system, or app store). What looks like a neutral prompt may be a carefully positioned continuation of the company’s own design.

The menu can preserve the gatekeeper

Nominal choice is choice in name. It gives the buyer a visible alternative without necessarily changing the conditions under which alternatives compete. If every listed service depends on one operating system, one account, one payment channel, or one approval process, the central power remains in place (even when every option is technically available).

That power can persist after the moment of selection. The gatekeeper may still decide which services are interoperable, which updates are permitted, which defaults return after an upgrade, and which costs attach to leaving. A person can select a rival and still encounter a system built to make the rival peripheral.

What does that choice mean if the selected service cannot reach the same users, use the same device functions, or compete on the same terms? The question is not whether an alternative appears on the screen. The question is whether the alternative can operate without asking the gatekeeper for special treatment.

A legal disclaimer won’t solve that problem. A disclaimer can describe a menu; it cannot create an open market. Nor can a company claim that every option is equal when its own defaults determine what people see first, what they learn to use, and what they must overcome to leave (the button the interface presents as normal).

A remedy must change control

A meaningful remedy would change the structure behind the screen. It would require access on fair terms to the functions and distribution routes that make a service viable (a company’s preferred route). It would limit the ability to reset a chosen default, bury a rival, or make switching costly through design. It would also require clear disclosure of who selected the options and what the gatekeeper still controls.

That remedy should not force every person to make a complicated decision at every turn. We’re asking for a market in which a simple choice has consequences beyond the appearance of choice. We’re also asking lawmakers to measure competition by what firms can do after selection, not by how many names fit inside a prompt.

The governing principle is straightforward: a choice screen is meaningful only when the choices can compete. If the system still controls access, defaults, data, and switching, the menu is a smokescreen (not merely a menu). Lawmakers should not impose remedies that leave that structure untouched, and they should not mistake a visible list for public control (including the cost of switching). If you want that principle enforced, contact the lawmakers responsible for the rules and ask what power the screen leaves in the gatekeeper’s hands.
